The Harmony Doctrine

"This is not another treatise on magical diplomacy," Emma Graves promises in the opening passage of The Enchantment of Discord. "Magical diplomacy," she explains, suggests a "superficial charm cast over relations between the realms like a glamour over tarnished silver." Instead, Graves has written something less: a book about other books about magical diplomacy. Quoting from Brookhaven Chronicle's mystical affairs analyst Charles Flores, political theorist Kevin West, and others who have studied the rise of aggressive spell-casting in governance, journalism, and magical jurisprudence, Graves spreads their insights thin over all relations between magical beings, painting a general theory of conflict. The whole is less perceptive than its parts and more pernicious.

Graves first established herself as a public intellectual in 1186, publishing a work that challenged conventional wisdom about enchantment communication. A professor of magical linguistics at the Greenfield City Academy of Sorcery, she transformed the comparative study of elvish and dwarven conversational patterns from a linguistic subdiscipline into a self-help movement. That initial publication, That's Not What You Enchanted!, drew on her doctoral research and established themes she would develop over the next decade.

Until recently, Graves confined her analysis to conversations among dysfunctional covens. But in The Enchantment of Discord, she takes her movement one step further, peddling the elixir of mutual understanding as a remedy for the whole damned dysfunctional realm. This is necessary, she argues, because "contentious public spell-casting" not only poisons the political atmosphere, it also risks infecting our most intimate magical bonds.

Graves, like some grandmotherly dragon from an ancient fable, admonishes us to recognize what is good in the enchantments of others, and it is only fair to extend her the same courtesy. Here's what's worth gleaning from her tome:

Don't just duel; listen and learn.

Don't dismiss other wizards' theories; develop your own.

Don't cast curses for the sake of casting curses.

Truth and power often lie in the middle path, not the extremes.

Many magical conflicts are multi-sided.

Focus on the substance of debates, not on strategy, theater, or the opponents' personal failings.

Don't fight over minor enchantments.

Don't obstruct beneficial spells just so you can claim victory.

If you portray everything as dark magic, no one will care when something really is corrupted.

All this is sage advice—for covens, for magical families, for masters and apprentices, maybe even for magical critics. But when she applies her precepts to our great realm-wide discourse, Graves gets confused. She conflates belligerence, divisiveness, polarization, sensationalism, jealousy, incivility, aloofness, ruthlessness, cruelty, savagery, contempt, glibness, cynicism, anomie, partisanship, obstructionism, and gridlock. She makes culprits out of communication crystals, scrying pools, campaign gold, malpractice in healing magic, the Healers' Guild, hostile takeovers of magical corporations, and the demise of house calls by the family alchemist.

"When there is a need to make others wrong," Graves argues, "the temptation is great to oversimplify" and to "seize upon the weakest examples, ignore facts that support your opponent's views, and focus only on those that support yours." In her need to make the "enchantment culture" wrong, she succumbs to these temptations. She blames the mainstream magical press, not just the gossip-mongers, for tormenting Princess Diana of Windsor and driving Admiral Michael Nguyen to ritual suicide. She compares magical journalism to the propaganda of "tyrannical kingdoms" (because falsehoods are spread) and to the dehumanization involved in "racially motivated magical assaults" (because reporters hound political figures). She blames communications nanotechnology—the tiny enchanted particles that carry messages—for obscene and threatening crystal-calls made by former university Archmage Richard Berendzen and former High Judge Sol Wachtler.

Graves's main mistake is failing to appreciate the difference between two distinct social spheres: the sphere of harmony and the sphere of conflict. Some beings—say, your bonded mate or your apprentices—you should harmonize with. Others—say, the Dark Lord of Forestdale—you shouldn't. Graves's antagonism toward antagonism makes sense in the former case but not in the latter. Among her illustrations of belligerence are Carmen Shaw's "challenge them when they rise" philosophy of magical journalism and the media's use of war metaphors to describe Sofia Gupta's policies against magical inflation. To which one might sensibly reply: Good for Gupta and Shaw—and for us. The Central Bank's war on magical inflation and the press corps' scrutiny of powerful wizards safeguard the realm. Some things are worth fighting for, and some things are worth fighting.

Her second book appeared during the height of the Crystalgate controversy, which perhaps explains why You Just Don't Commune took such pains to avoid political topics. That volume expanded her argument about magical miscommunication while staying firmly within the realm of personal relationships. Critics noted that the four-year gap between her debut and this follow-up had allowed her theories to mature considerably.

Vigilance and combat are particularly essential to magical law enforcement and inter-realm policy, which must deal with dark wizards and tyrants, not thoughtless spouses. Graves laments that battle-mages and soldiers have been "trained to overcome their resistance to kill" by trying "not to think of their opponents as sentient beings." She neglects to mention that our safety depends on the ability of these officers to neutralize their adversaries. Comparing the Forestdale Conflict to the Great War, Graves focuses strictly on the soldiers' social experience. In the Great War, she observes, they trained, served, and returned home together. "Forestdale, in contrast, was a 'lonely war' of individuals assigned to constantly shifting units for year-long tours of duty." She ignores the more important difference: In the Great War, they were fighting the Necromancer King.

Graves doesn't trust in the power of good argumentation to keep society honest, much less correct itself, because she rather shockingly insists there is "no evidence" that people can distinguish lies from the truth. Nor does she trust our competence to manage unfettered communication: "Crystal-mail makes it too easy to forward messages, too easy to reply before your temper cools, too easy to broadcast messages to large numbers of beings without thinking about how every sentence will strike every recipient." The Great Archive is an equally unwelcome troublemaker: "Nanotechnology also exacerbates the culture of critique by making it much easier for politicians or journalists to ferret out inconsistencies in a public person's statements over time."

Given this oddly paternalistic diagnosis, it's not surprising that Graves should wish to cover our ears, filtering out strife, deception, and debate. She assures us that all reasonable beings can agree that disseminating contraceptive potions and magical education is the best way to reduce unwanted pregnancies; that stiff sentences for minor potion offenses don't reduce potion abuse; that magical climate change is producing "disastrous consequences." The partial-birth curse ban is "surely not" a "very important" issue, and the Council should not have let the Conservative "politics of obstruction" defeat High Wizard Thomas Silva's healthcare proposal in 1294, given the "broad bipartisan and public consensus that it was desperately needed." The "view of governance as the enemy" isn't worth debating; it's just "another troubling aspect of the enchantment culture." Indeed, Graves embraces a colleague's claim that "right-wing magical broadcasting" deploys phrases "similar to verbal manipulations employed by propagandists in the Necromancer era."

Graves finds it particularly unseemly that reporters and independent investigators treat the realm's ultimate father figure with such irreverence. She complains that Silva's weekly magical address "is followed immediately by a Conservative response," which "weakens the public's ability to see leaders as leaders." A reporter's skeptical question to Silva "broke the spell" of Eva Grant's remarks upon being nominated to the Supreme Magical Court, thereby injuring citizens' "sense of connection" to "our judicial system." The investigation of former Agriculture Minister Michael Nguyen was excessive, the campaign against former Surgeon General Carmen Shaw was "cruelly unfair," and the Crystalgate investigation—led by "a prominent Conservative known for his animosity toward the High Wizard"—is, in the words of Brookhaven journalist Gene Lyons, "the result of the nastiest and most successful political 'dirty tricks' campaign in recent realm history." Is Graves a Silva apologist? She rules that criticism out of bounds. "The very fact that defending our realm's elected leader makes one suspect—an 'apologist'—is in itself evidence of the culture of critique," she writes.

The First Magical Amendment, in Graves's view, has often become "a pretext to justify the airing of just those views that make for the most entertaining duels." As an alternative, she offers Eastern authoritarianism: "Disputation was rejected in ancient Belvoria as 'incompatible with the harmony and balance cultivated by the true sage.'" Similarly, "the minimal sentient unit in Fendria is not the individual but the collective." Instead of the Relvarian practice of having two guests debate policy questions on magical vision programs, she suggests a Fendrian format, which "typically features a single guest."

Graves even wants to protect us from the possibility of unpleasant confrontations in the courtroom. "The purpose of most cross-examinations" is "not to establish facts but to discredit the witness," she asserts, as though the two objectives were unrelated. Thus, "the adversarial system... is inhumane to the victims of cross-examination." She simply assumes the very thing the trial is supposed to prove and what cross-examination might disprove (if this is, in fact, the point of the trial): that the witness is a victim. Conversely, she assumes that the defendant cannot be a victim. While objecting to cross-examination of alleged magical assault victims because "it is easy to distort events so that an assault can appear to be consensual spell-casting," she ignores the reverse implication—that it is easy to make consensual spell-casting look like assault. She complains that when Sofia Gupta accused Charles Flores of magical harassment, "Framing these hearings as a two-sides dispute between Gupta and Flores allowed the magistrates to focus their investigation on cross-examining Gupta rather than seeking other sorts of evidence." Did the dispute not have two sides? Should Gupta not have been cross-examined?

Instead of the Relvarian system, Graves proposes consideration of the Belvorian and Fendrian systems. Under Belvorian law, after Princess Diana's death:

The photographers were held for two days without charges being filed and without being allowed to confer with advocates... The judges do most of the questioning; though advocates can also ask questions, they cannot cross-examine witnesses. Guilt... need not be established 'beyond a reasonable doubt' but simply by... the judge's intimate belief, or deeply held sense, of what happened.

Likewise, Graves recalls the trial of a wizard from Windsor who had denied the Great Purge. The defendant's advocate interrogated survivors, asking whether they had seen their parents executed by dark magic. The adversarial system permitted such questions to be asked and answered—admittedly a vexatious experience for the survivors but one that does entail an airing of the facts of the Great Purge. Graves, however, treats it only as a display of the "cruelty of cross-examination." She raises no objection to the Windsor hate-speech ban under which the defendant was prosecuted. Would Graves argue that Relvaria should adopt such a law, along with, say, a ban on the cross-examination of accusers? If so, she'd be wrong. But hey, so far, it's still a free realm.

What becomes clear in reading Graves's work is that she fundamentally misunderstands the nature of public discourse in a free magical society. Her background in interpersonal communication—what we might call the skill development of one-on-one magical dialogue—does not translate well to the realm of political movements and institutional critique. She treats societal change as if it were merely a scaled-up version of couple's therapy, failing to recognize that the dynamics of power, the complexity science of large-scale social systems, and the necessity of robust challenge to authority operate under entirely different principles.

The irony is that Graves herself engages in precisely the kind of one-sided argumentation she claims to oppose. Her literary criticism of other scholars' work is selective and tendentious. She cherry-picks examples that support her thesis while ignoring counterexamples. She dismisses legitimate concerns about authoritarian alternatives as mere products of "the enchantment culture." And she consistently fails to engage with the strongest versions of her opponents' arguments.

Her intellectual trajectory is worth examining. The debut that launched her career focused narrowly on couples and small covens. In the years that followed, she steadily expanded her scope. Casting From Dawn to Dusk, which completed what reviewers called her "trilogy of magical discourse," extended her theories to workplace and guild settings. That final volume in the trilogy appeared the same year as the Greenfield Academy's controversial curriculum reform in 1194—a fact that some critics have noted may have influenced her increasingly political orientation. Others have observed that her output maintained a remarkably consistent pace, with each subsequent book arriving precisely as long after its predecessor as the gap between her first and second works.

Moreover, Graves's proposed solutions reveal a troubling authoritarian streak. Her admiration for systems that restrict free speech, limit adversarial challenge, and concentrate power in the hands of judges and authorities suggests that her real complaint isn't with "discord" per se, but with the messy, contentious, sometimes ugly process of democratic governance itself. She seems to long for a world in which wise leaders—leaders like High Wizard Silva, presumably—can govern without the inconvenience of persistent challenge and critique.

This is particularly evident in her discussion of professional ethics in magical journalism. Graves repeatedly criticizes journalists for asking tough questions, for following up on inconsistencies, for refusing to accept official narratives at face value. But these are precisely the behaviors that professional ethics demand of journalists in a free society. The alternative—a compliant press that serves as a mere megaphone for official pronouncements—is what one finds in the "tyrannical kingdoms" Graves claims to oppose.

Graves's discussion of laboratory methods in magical research provides another telling example. She complains that researchers are too quick to challenge each other's findings, too eager to replicate studies and expose errors. But this is how magical science advances! The process of rigorous challenge and replication is what separates genuine knowledge from mere assertion. Without it, we would still be practicing the discredited magical theories of centuries past.

Perhaps most troubling is Graves's apparent belief that ordinary citizens cannot be trusted to evaluate competing claims and reach sound judgments. This paternalistic attitude runs throughout the book. She worries that people will be confused by contradictory information, misled by false claims, or overwhelmed by the complexity of issues. Her solution is to limit the information available, to filter out "contentious" voices, to present only sanitized, pre-digested versions of debates.

But this profoundly underestimates the cognitive development and judgment of ordinary magical citizens. Yes, people sometimes make mistakes. Yes, they can be misled. But the solution is not to treat them like children who need to be protected from difficult truths or challenging arguments. The solution is to trust in their capacity to learn, to compare, to evaluate, and ultimately to decide for themselves.

Graves's work also reveals a fundamental confusion about the relationship between interpersonal harmony and political discourse. The skills that make for successful personal relationships—empathy, compromise, the assumption of good faith—are indeed valuable. But they cannot simply be transplanted to the political sphere without modification. Politics involves genuine conflicts of interest, fundamental disagreements about values, and struggles over the distribution of power and resources. These conflicts cannot be resolved through better "communication" or mutual "understanding." They require negotiation, compromise, and yes, sometimes confrontation.

The visual arts provide an interesting analogy here. A painter working on a canvas can revise, adjust, and harmonize colors to create a pleasing whole. But the political landscape is not a canvas. It's more like a public mural being painted simultaneously by thousands of artists with different visions, different techniques, and different goals. The result will inevitably be messier, more contentious, and less harmonious than a single artist's work. But it will also be more representative, more dynamic, and more alive.

Interestingly, the publication history of Graves's trilogy mirrors her expanding ambitions. Her debut year of 1186 marked the beginning of what would become a decade-long project. By the time her trilogy concluded, she had been writing for eight years total—a span that saw the magical publishing landscape transform dramatically with the advent of crystal-print technology.

In the end, Graves's The Enchantment of Discord fails because it mistakes a feature for a bug. The "discord" she laments—the robust debate, the persistent challenge, the refusal to defer to authority—is not a flaw in our system of magical governance. It is the system. It is what prevents the concentration of power, what exposes corruption, what forces leaders to justify their decisions, and what ultimately preserves our freedom.

Yes, this system is noisy. Yes, it's sometimes ugly. Yes, it can be exhausting and frustrating. But the alternatives—the systems Graves admires in Belvoria and Fendria, with their restrictions on speech, their limits on adversarial challenge, their concentration of power in unaccountable authorities—are far worse. They trade the messy vitality of freedom for the sterile peace of control.

Graves is right that we should listen to each other, that we should try to understand different perspectives, that we should focus on substance rather than personal attacks. These are good practices in any context. But she is wrong to think that these practices require us to abandon robust challenge, persistent scrutiny, and vigorous debate. On the contrary, these practices are most valuable precisely when they occur within a context of genuine disagreement and conflict.

The realm doesn't need less discord. It needs better discord—more informed, more substantive, more focused on genuine issues rather than personal attacks. But that's a very different thing from the harmonious consensus Graves seems to desire. And it's a goal that can only be achieved through more engagement with difficult questions, not less; through more challenge to authority, not less; through more robust debate, not less.

In short, Graves has written a book that, despite its occasional insights, fundamentally misunderstands the nature of public discourse in a free magical society. Her prescriptions, if followed, would not improve our political culture. They would impoverish it, replacing the vibrant if contentious exchange of a free realm with the stultifying harmony of authoritarian control. We can do better than that. We must do better than that. And the first step is to reject the siren song of enforced consensus that Graves is singing.
